title: Understanding the Evidence Base on AI in K-12 Education (scale.stanford.edu), March 11, 2026, 3.20.26
author: Stanford SCALE Initiative
source: Research in Action, SCALE Initiative, Stanford Graduate School of Education
summary: Stanford's SCALE Initiative reviews the rapidly growing research literature on AI in K-12 education and finds that, despite more than 800 published papers in its Research Repository, only 20 meet the bar of rigorous, causal-impact studies of how AI tools actually affect students or educators. The report finds that student performance often improves while using AI tools but the evidence is mixed once support is removed, raising the question of whether AI is building durable skills or just helping students complete tasks. It highlights that tools with pedagogical guardrails -- tutoring systems that scaffold reasoning -- show more promise than general-purpose chatbots that hand over answers directly, and it uses established learning-science frameworks (cognitive load theory, zone of proximal development, metacognition, desirable difficulties, the expertise reversal effect) to interpret why. The review also finds emerging evidence that AI can help teachers by reducing lesson-prep time and surfacing real-time instructional feedback. Major gaps remain: there are no high-quality causal studies of student AI use conducted in actual U.S. K-12 classrooms, most research examines only short-term outcomes, and almost nothing has been studied about AI's effects on equity, wellness, or social development. The report's core argument is that education leaders should ground AI adoption and procurement decisions in this thin but growing evidence base rather than in hype or vendor claims.
points: Of more than 800-1,100 papers in the AI Hub Research Repository, only 20 are high-quality causal-impact studies -- most published research on AI in education is technical/computational or descriptive, not evidence of actual effect on learning.

AI tools built with pedagogical guardrails (tutoring systems that scaffold and give hints) show more promising causal outcomes than general-purpose chatbots that simply generate answers, a finding the report ties directly to cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect.

A recurring pattern across studies is that performance gains often disappear once AI support is removed, which the report frames as an open question about whether AI use builds durable skill or just tool-dependent task completion.

There are currently zero high-quality causal studies of student AI use conducted in real U.S. K-12 classrooms, and almost no research on AI's impact on equity, student wellness, or social development -- a major blind spot given how fast adoption is moving.

Early causal evidence suggests AI can meaningfully help teachers by reducing time spent on lesson preparation and surfacing real-time, messaging-based instructional suggestions, without degrading instructional quality.
quotes: AI tools are arriving in schools faster than research can evaluate them. Teachers are experimenting with new tools and districts are writing policies, all while students are already using AI both inside and outside the classroom.

However, most of this research does not evaluate impact. After reviewing the full repository, we identified only 20 high-quality causal studies that rigorously examine how AI tools affect students or educators.

Many studies find that students perform better on tasks like math practice, programming assignments, or writing when they can use AI tools during the activity. Evidence across the causal studies is mixed when students complete assessments without AI support.

Across the causal studies reviewed, evidence suggests that AI tools designed with pedagogical guardrails – such as tutoring systems that give hints or guide reasoning – show more promising outcomes than general-purpose chatbots that provide answers directly.
While these early findings are informative, the evidence base has major gaps.

By synthesizing the strongest available studies, the report aims to give educators, school leaders, policymakers, and researchers a clearer starting point for making decisions in a rapidly evolving landscape.
